content: A previous version of this Cochrane Review demonstrated that insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) are effective in reducing child mortality, the prevalence of malaria parasites, and the incidence of both uncomplicated and severe malaria episodes. Since then, ITNs have become a cornerstone of malaria control efforts, significantly contributing to the substantial decline in malaria cases and deaths observed since the early 2000s. However, during this same period, resistance to pyrethroids—the insecticide used in ITNs—has increased, raising concerns about whether findings from earlier trials, conducted before widespread resistance, remain applicable to current malaria transmission dynamics. The primary aim of this updated review was to evaluate the impact of ITNs on mortality and malaria-related morbidity, incorporating new evidence published since the last update. The certainty of the evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and cluster RCTs that compared ITNs treated with synthetic pyrethroids at WHO-recommended doses to either no nets or untreated nets. Data were analyzed using risk ratios (RRs), rate ratios, and mean differences, with results presented alongside 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The updated search identified three new trials, bringing the total to 23 trials conducted between 1987 and 2001, involving over 275,793 participants. The findings are as follows: 1. ITNs versus No Nets: ITNs reduce all-cause child mortality by 17% compared to no nets (rate ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.89; 5 trials, 200,833 participants, high-certainty evidence). This equates to saving 5.6 lives (95% CI 3.6 to 7.6) annually for every 1,000 children protected with ITNs. ITNs reduce the incidence of uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria episodes by nearly half (rate ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.64; 5 trials, 35,551 participants, high-certainty evidence). ITNs likely reduce the incidence of uncomplicated Plasmodium vivax malaria episodes (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.77; 2 trials, 10,967 participants, moderate-certainty evidence). ITNs reduce the prevalence of P. falciparum malaria by 17% compared to no nets (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.98; 6 trials, 18,809 participants, high-certainty evidence). However, they may have little or no effect on the prevalence of P. vivax malaria (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.34; 2 trials, 10,967 participants, low-certainty evidence). ITNs reduce the incidence of severe malaria episodes by 44% (rate ratio 0.56, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.82; 2 trials, 31,173 participants, high-certainty evidence). ITNs increase mean hemoglobin levels (measured as mean packed cell volume) compared to no nets (mean difference 1.29, 95% CI 0.42 to 2.16; 5 trials, 11,489 participants, high-certainty evidence). 2. ITNs versus Untreated Nets: ITNs likely reduce all-cause child mortality by approximately one-third compared to untreated nets (rate ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.36 to 1.23; 2 trials, 25,389 participants, moderate-certainty evidence). This corresponds to saving 3.5 lives (95% CI -2.4 to 6.8) annually for every 1,000 children protected with ITNs. ITNs reduce the incidence of uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria episodes (rate ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.78; 5 trials, 2,036 participants, high-certainty evidence). ITNs may reduce the incidence of uncomplicated P. vivax malaria episodes (rate ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.05; 3 trials, 1,535 participants, low-certainty evidence). ITNs likely reduce P. falciparum prevalence by 10% compared to untreated nets (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.05; 3 trials, 2,259 participants, moderate-certainty evidence). However, the impact of ITNs on P. vivax prevalence remains unclear (1 trial, 350 participants, very low-certainty evidence). The effect of ITNs on mean packed cell volume is also uncertain (2 trials, 1,909 participants, low-certainty evidence). The authors concluded that while there is some evidence suggesting that insecticide resistance affects mosquito mortality, the quantitative significance of this effect remains unclear. The available evidence was deemed insufficient to downgrade the strong benefits of ITNs on mortality and malaria illness observed in earlier trials.
